en: It is said that a consciousness which does not take coarse characteristics as its object takes subtle characteristics as its sphere. The *Saṃyukta-āgama* states:

"Some say that the consciousness of yours which takes the coarse characteristics of a jar as its object is itself the consciousness which takes subtle characteristics as its object. If you grant this, then the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is:
your consciousness which takes color-form as its object should also take sound as its object; thus, you would be admitting that mutually exclusive phenomena are attained."
Because both are taken as objects,
the fault of the unestablished probandum (*asiddha*) in this illustrative analogy regarding coarse and subtle objects does not apply.
The claim that "the coarse and subtle minds do not serve as an analogy because they do not take sound and so forth as their objects,
and because those coarse and subtle objects are not sound and so forth" is incorrect;
this refutation does not follow the original commentary as stated in the *Liang*.
The *Benshu* (Original Commentary) on the *Pramāṇa* states:
"Regarding your other objects, such as sound and so forth,
the consciousness that takes other objects, such as visible form, should likewise be able to take them as its objects."
This is because it is admitted that mutually contradictory phenomena can take one another as simultaneous objects. Here, the subject (*dharmin*) is the other objects such as sound,
and the predicate (*dharma*) is the mind that takes those other visible forms as its object.
The objective sphere of form is both non-dharmic and dharmic.
It is the mind that apprehends the object and takes form as its condition;
it is the mind of sound that constitutes a contrary condition.
This contrary mind should also be able to take [the object] as its focal point;
this is precisely the nature of that phenomenon, because it is admitted that contrary phenomena can be simultaneously taken as focal points. This is the reason.
As in the analogy of the coarse and the subtle,
because two [distinct] positions are established, inference (*anumāna*) is valid;
otherwise, it would follow that a consciousness directed toward one object could take another object as its cognitive domain.
Ximing says: "The word 'wu' means 'mo.
'Mo' refers to both coarse and subtle objects."
Because there would be the fault of confusion.
If it is not admitted that [the consciousness] takes as its object a sphere characterized by roundness and subtlety,
then the original roundness and subtlety should not be among the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
If you concede that this contradicts your own tenet,
then a single consciousness should be able to take all objects as its conditions;
if a consciousness that takes coarse objects can also take subtle characteristics as its conditions, [then why not all?].
A mind that takes blue and so forth as its object should likewise take sound and so forth as its object;
thus, visual consciousness and the other sensory consciousnesses would all equally take the eighteen dhātus as their objects. The *Ji* states:
"Some say this is a subsequent measure [of proof]."
There are those who understand that both types of valid cognition possess faults;
for this reason, some offer an interpretation that refutes [the opponent] solely through reasoning.
It is not a refutation by means of a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*). This is also not the case.
What fault would there be in refuting that [opponent] by means of a formal syllogism?
For now, let us set forth a syllogism as follows:
Your sound-object should be the object-condition for other contradictory cognitions,
because you admit that contradictory phenomena can be apprehended simultaneously.
Just as with coarse and subtle objects,
this sound also has coarse and subtle aspects,
because it is apprehended by contradictory cognitions.
There are three characteristics of the cause (*hetu*).
This explains the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
Furthermore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (72), there are two other characteristics.
First, the characteristic of the fundamental nature;
second, the characteristic of the reflected image.
What is the characteristic of the fundamental nature?
This refers to that which is produced from prior conceptualization,
that which is produced from signs, and the characteristics established through their combination.
What is the characteristic of an image?
It refers to that which arises from pervasive conceptualization and is manifested through resolute conviction;
it does not abide in its own fundamental nature. The *Ji* (Commentary) states:
That which is established in common refers to the function of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
that is to say, it is due to the power of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the perfuming agent.
The objective aspect (nimittabhāga) can perfume the seeds of both the ālayavijñāna’s seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga) and its own objective aspect;
this is not the case for the resultant (vipāka) mind and mental factors,
as they lack the capacity to perfume.
The marks (*nimitta*) also do not perfuse [the seeds].
Therefore, it is said that "first, there is discrimination," and so forth. Now, this is explained:
regarding those seventy-two things mentioned as "marks."
It is not merely the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
If that which is expressed by a name is collectively termed a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*),
then as previously stated, the seven consciousnesses are also called the "characteristic of the fundamental nature" (*prakṛti-lakṣaṇa*).
Because both take the sixth consciousness as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
they consist of the seeds existing from the beginning (*mūla-bīja*) produced by prior discrimination,
as well as the newly perfumed seeds (*navābhyasta-bīja*) produced by characteristics.
Because they share the same essential nature,
they are said to have a "commonly established characteristic.
Otherwise, the essential nature is spoken of in terms of its active manifestation (*pravṛtti*).
Since the seeds that subsequently produce the manifesting portion have long since ceased,
how can it be said that they constitute a "mutually established characteristic"?
Nor can it be said that this is stated based on the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The treatise states: "First, those produced by discrimination and those produced by characteristics.
If one were to rely on the perspective of predominance (*adhipati*), it should state: "First, those produced by discrimination and those produced by characteristics."
Furthermore, this constitutes the meaning of "conjunction.
Since each is said to arise,
it clarifies that they are distinct seeds.
Some say that "yoga-master" (yogācārya) is an *upapada* compound (*tatpuruṣa*),
while "master who possesses yoga" (*yogavān ācāryaḥ*) is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). This too is an *upapada* compound,
and not a possessive one, as distinguished previously.
Later, the *Cheng weishi lun shuji* (Commentary on the Demonstration of Consciousness-Only) states: "The meaning of the correspondence between mind and object is difficult to comprehend for now.
If one says that the arising of the mind must necessarily rely upon an object..."
The mind tends toward this object,
and the object accords with that mind;
therefore, they are called "associated."
The objects of perception should all be accessible across the three natures within both concentrated and distracted states of mind.
If it is argued that the object necessarily manifests according to what the mind desires,
and is thus called "associated" because of mastery over it:
If one analyzes aggregated form through conceptual imagination,
even though one achieves a subtle understanding, the subtle does not actually appear;
how, then, can such a person be called a yogācāra?
If it is argued that the mind is "associated" because it does not contradict the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the phenomena that constitute its objects,
then one would be conceiving of atoms where none previously existed within the primary mass of form.
How do they correspond? Because they destroy the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The commentary on the *Ji* (集) itself explains:
Observing that the objects perceived by the contemplative mind do not obstruct that contemplative mind,
one causes the various modes of understanding and practice of that contemplative mind—
such as the colors blue and yellow or the characteristics of atoms— to function with mastery.
Therefore, it is called the "concordance of mind and object" (*cittālambana-saṃprayoga*).
It is not that the characteristics of the object appear in accordance with the mind that they are called "concordant. This is also not the case;
for although a flower in the sky does not exist, [it nonetheless appears].
Nor does it obstruct the mind from forming the conception of empty flowers;
just as when a disease impairs the eyes, one sees yellow where there is no yellow, the objects of our pervasive conceptualization— such as the self and so forth—
all fail to obstruct the arising of the mind's false and deluded conceptions.
How could it be said that mind and object are "associated"?
Therefore, we know that what is called "association" (saṃprayoga) means that the mind accords with the object; this is termed association.
This accords with the meaning of conformity.
Although the aggregate lacks atoms,
by relying on the sacred teachings and contemplating it through conceptual designation, one enters into accord with non-self.
That the objective realm of the principle of selflessness and the objective realm of the verbal teachings correspond with the mind is a sound explanation.
One should consult the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (the twentieth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*), and the *Yogācāra-bhūmi-ṭīkā*.
Question: When gross material forms are gradually analyzed and deconstructed until they reach the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), [what occurs]?
"Why not [allow for] seeds to be formed through distinct perfuming?

Answer: "Because there is no objective basis (ālambana-prakṛti). If that is so, then when seeds are formed through the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*), or through the perfuming of objects previously experienced, [how can this be explained?]"
How can there be a substantial entity? Answer: It is like the perfuming by names and phrases, and the perception of past objects.
Because those objects previously existed, they can give rise [to cognition];
thus, seeds are perfumed and established.
A flower in the sky does not exist; although it serves as a condition, it cannot separately infuse a seed.
Subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) are likewise:

since their substance is fundamentally non-existent, they do not separately infuse [seeds]. Question: Since a flower in the sky lacks substance, it may indeed not infuse seeds. However, [subtle atoms] do possess substance; why then do they not infuse [seeds]?
Question: Why do atoms (*paramāṇu*), which rely upon matter (*rūpa*), not constitute seeds? Answer:
Although they exist within the characteristics of matter, because they are grasped as a self (*ātman*) and so forth, they do not constitute seeds. It is not otherwise;
for that grasping does not perceive the atom as an object of grasping.
Question: What serves as the analogy? Answer: Although it is not a mind of grasping, because it lacks a substantial form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it does not serve as an analogy.
If one follows the Master of Ximing, he would allow that it constitutes a seed (*bīja*).
This has been refuted as before.
The treatise refutes the Saṃmitīya school by stating:

"Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish without depending on a cause. Question: How is it known that the characteristic of cessation in the Mahāyāna does not depend on a cause? Answer: The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states:
Furthermore, it is like boiling water until it reaches its minimum state, after which no more water arises;
yet this is not because the water ceases to exist only upon contact with fire. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
Because it is admitted that this is cessation, just like unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) cessation; according to this,
it appears as if a functional phenomenon (bhāva-dharma) is being taken as the cause.
If there were a dharma that serves as a cause, then no dharma would exist;
thus, there would be the fault of the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
The explanation says: cessation has many forms of cessation.
Taking conditioned phenomena as subject, one asserts their movement and cessation,
using other forms of cessation as the reason,
while taking up only a partial aspect thereof.

Therefore, there is likewise no fault. Question: Can unconditioned cessation (asaṃskṛta-nirodha) be equated with conditioned [cessation]? Answer: It is simply stated in general that it is admitted to be cessation;
thus, there is no need to differentiate between the cessation of essence (svabhāva-nirodha) and the cessation of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-nirodha).
Since the unconditioned does not depend on causes,
the conditioned likewise should not depend on them; therefore,
one cannot differentiate between them by means of causes.
Furthermore, for example, sound is impermanent;
that which is impermanent is subject to cessation.
Yet, one speaks of "impermanence."
It does not merely express the characteristic of cessation.
The *Exposition of the Teachings* (14) states:
"As for the nature of impermanence..."
This refers to their association with the three conditioned characteristics:
first, the characteristic of arising;
second, the characteristic of cessation.
Third is the characteristic of change.
These three characteristics are collectively termed "impermanence.
Furthermore, arising is said to function as a causal nature.
This cessation is also like that. The *Yaoji* states: "There are some who measure [the matter] thus:
the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) should not depend upon a cause."
Because names cease, it is like analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Some state the following syllogism:
Your cessation should not depend on a cause,
because you admit it is a cessation, just like the cessation of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Ji says: These two masters’ analogies suffer from the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the thesis (*asiddha-sādhya*).
That is to say, although the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) lack the sense of arising, [the analogy still fails].
Because they both depend on causes for their manifestation, they are both termed "dependent on causes.

In the thesis, one should state that [unconditioned phenomena] are not extinguished by depending on a cause of extinction; this is also not the case, for the essence of the unconditioned is itself extinction.
Cessation is not designated as "cessation" only because it is manifested by depending on causes;
rather, its very nature is cessation, and for that reason it is called "cessation.
Therefore, it is said: "Since it does not depend on causes, the analogy is established."
It is not that there is nothing established;
the treatise does not manifest odor or taste. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states:
Your [position that] visible color, as well as odor and taste,
should not be informative,
because they are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Just as with earth, water, and fire,
although they possess fragrance and taste according to their own nature,
these are merely conventional designations.
It does not apply to wholesome or unwholesome [matter].
Since intention is what destroys others, the manifest karma of matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) is likewise wholesome or unwholesome;
for they themselves admit that the three—odor, taste, and tangibility—are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, according to the treatise and its commentary, it should be stated:

"This informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) of yours is also not manifest color (*varṇa*), nor is it odor or taste, because it lacks informative expression (*avijñapti*), just like tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*); for this is what [the opponent] admits."
Regarding the argument that sound in a single moment lacks expressive power:
the Sarvāstivādins maintain that this expression is real.
Now, let us inquire:
do the names and so forth produced by sound constitute a real expressive function from the very first moment that the sound is produced?
If names and so forth were to truly express their meaning only when produced by the final momentary sound,
then if the first [sound] were capable [of expression], the subsequent ones would be useless.
If it is capable later,
then the inference is as follows:
"Your sound of the subsequent single moment [is impermanent]."
Apart from the Buddha’s mind, it could not possibly express [the meaning], because it is sound,
just like the sound of the very first moment.
If it is argued that [sound] exists as a continuum, this is refuted later;
for according to their fundamental tenet, with the exception of the Buddha, no other person possesses sound for even a single moment.
It is not that which expresses [meaning]. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (15) states:
"Śrāvakas can express a single syllable through many moments of sound."
A single moment of sound from a Buddha can express a single syllable;
yet within the sound of that single syllable, there is still no collection of names or phrases.
Therefore, it cannot convey meaning. Question: For what reason is "informative form" (vijñapti-rūpa) established separately among the categories of form?
Question: Why is "informative intimation" (*vijñapti*) not established among sounds? Answer: Informative intimation is established separately because material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are manifest;
however, because the characteristics of sound are difficult to discern, it is not established separately.

Furthermore, categories such as square, round, long, and short can also be known [in sound]. Another explanation is that within the category of color-form (*varṇa-rūpa*), there exists shape-form (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) that is not informative intimation.
Within the category of form (*rūpa*), "informative" (*vijñapti*) is established separately.
Among sounds, those that are vocal (*vāc*) are necessarily informative;
since there are no non-informative sounds, they are not established separately. Question: Does the bodily informative form (*kāya-vijñapti-rūpa*) depend upon the body?
From that which is based on the name-body (*nāmakāya*), there is the expression of speech; the expression of speech is also based on the body.
From that which is based on the name-body, [it follows that] the answer is that visible form (*saṃsthāna*) is not separate from the body.
Because it follows its basis and is named "bodily intimation" (*kāyavijñapti*),
yet its nature as sound issues forth detached from the substance [of the body] and is coarse,
it is not bodily intimation. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that bodily intimation occurs at the initial moment.

This follows from the fact that vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*) was explained after bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*); it is mentioned last for fear of being confused with what is not bodily intimation.
Now, based on the distinctions between wholesome and unwholesome intentions and aspirations,
I shall set forth the correct interpretation below,
dividing it into three parts.
The first section concerns the general categories of the path, meditative discipline (*samādhi-saṃvara*), non-discipline (*asaṃvara*), and that which is intermediate (*madhyama*).
The second section concerns the specific category of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of the Buddha’s body. Next, it is said that this may depend on the lower [levels].
These are other specific explanations; they are distinct phrases concerning the intermediate state, or they depend on the lower levels within meditative concentration.
They are distinct phrases concerning concentration and the path, because for a Buddha there is no further increase.
Because, with the exception of the Buddha, other types such as those of separate liberation increase;
and because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*) depend upon the present.
Question: Is the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) established based on the seeds of manifest action (*vijñapti*)?

Question: Since there are multiple moments of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*), upon which moment is the [informative] manifestation (*vijñapti*) established? Answer: It is established upon the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates bodily or vocal action at the first moment;
this may occur simultaneously with the action or sequentially before or after it.
When simultaneous, they share the same seed;
when occurring sequentially, each has its own distinct seed;
in both cases, they are established upon the initial [moment].
From the second moment onward,
it is not the causal motivation (hetu-samutthāna),
but is merely termed the momentary motivation (kṣaṇa-samutthāna).

Because it is not fundamental. Question: Since it is admitted that bodily and vocal actions arise within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), upon what is their manifestation (*vijñapti*) established?
If it is the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates movement, then that would be a present state of concentration.
This meditative absorption is accompanied by both [informative and non-informative action]. Answer: Since these are established as conventional designations, what prevents them from applying to both?
However, according to the Sarvāstivāda, those that follow the mind—namely, the two types of restraint consisting of the Path and Meditative Absorption—are such.
If there is mind, it exists;
if there is no mind, it does not exist.
Abandoning this concentration, one takes up another concentration.
One abandons this non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) and acquires that non-informative matter;
the same applies to the Path (*mārga*).
In all cases, there exists a distinct, substantial form of matter called non-informative matter.
One does not grasp at the two associated thoughts of concentration and the path.
Furthermore, concentration is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*);
that which is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is termed the "path."
If the Mahāyāna masters follow this same sense,
yet they establish a distinction:
it is established based on volition (*cetanā*) that manifests simultaneously with both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*).
The meditative supernormal powers (dhyānābhijñā) are untainted (anāsrava); although they consist of a single volition (cetanā), they differ according to their intended purpose.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the eight precepts (aṣṭāṅga-śīla) must be received from another and possess all their constituent parts (sakalāṅga).
This alone is the day and night;
it encompasses all Mahāyāna,
whether one follows a teacher or not.
Whether the supports are complete or incomplete,
and whether it lasts for one day or many days,
neither case constitutes a violation.
Because it is established according to the limits of one's intention and vow,
the Buddha, in his pedagogical discourse, spoke of "one day and night" merely as a means to facilitate learning.
In the Mahāyāna, the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions may also be received even if some branches are temporarily omitted; however,
only the ordained community may receive them by relying on a teacher, with all branches complete and for the duration of their lives.
However, those cases where the branches are omitted all refer to the period prior to the recitation of the Three Refuges;
they may be omitted because there is a distinct aspiration [for a specific goal]. This applies to such practices as the three clusters of precepts and the ten inexhaustible vows.
Furthermore, according to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchāprajñāpāramitāsūtra*,
those who receive the ten precepts are identical to śrāmaṇeras who observe the ten precepts.
Nevertheless, it is also received until the end of the future.
Furthermore, there are four distinctions regarding this attainment of precepts:
first, attainment with a mind, which refers to those who give rise to a superior wholesome mind through making aspirational vows; second, non-attainment with a mind.
This refers to not generating the aspiration [to receive the precepts].

Even if one generates the aspiration and receives the Prātimokṣa vows of the monastic community, if there is only a limited duration, or if the constituent branches are deficient, or if the intention is incomplete, one does not obtain the precepts. Third, they cannot be obtained by one who lacks a mind.

This refers to the case where an Anāgāmin śrāmaṇera, having resolved to seek the precepts and completed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), enters the concentration of non-mentation (*acittaka-samādhi*).
While in this state of non-mentation, the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is concluded.
Because his aspiration was fulfilled, he also obtains full ordination (*upasampadā*). However, one cannot obtain [the precepts] during the four states of non-mentation.

This refers to the state of being without mind other than the state of having no aspiration. Question: The unmanifest (avijñapti) of prātimokṣa is established based upon the seeds of volition that initiate action;
for example, one obtains the prātimokṣa precepts upon entering the path of seeing (darśanamārga).

Question: Since [the body] does not arise [at that moment], upon what kind of volition (*cetanā*) is speech established? Answer: Prior to entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is a mind of aspiration that moves and initiates the body;
subsequently, upon entering the path of seeing, it is established based on this seed.

If it were not so, there would be no [unmanifest action] at all. Question: The unmanifest actions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*) depend upon deliberate and decisive volition (*cetanā*).

When bodily or vocal actions arise, upon what kind of volition are they established as bodily or vocal karma? Answer: If bodily or vocal actions arise within other types of meditative concentration, they are the "fruition of supernormal powers" (*abhijñā-phala*).
Furthermore, in the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) prior to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is a mind of aspiration desiring to initiate bodily and vocal actions.

Although the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) induced by concentration do not exist in the state of non-concentration (*vikṣepa*), nor are they present during the actual concentration itself, the volition (*cetanā*) that moves and initiates them arises nonetheless for the sake of producing bodily and vocal actions. Question: At the time of initiating the preparatory stage, one merely possesses a deliberative and decisive volition; has the impelling [volition] not yet arisen?
How is this established? Answer: Based on the actual fact, within meditative absorption (samādhi), there arises movement and the initiation of volition (cetanā).
For example, from the eighth stage (bhūmi) upward, one is constantly in a state of meditative mind;
it is in this sense that it is said to be different from the state of distraction.
Regarding whether the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome actions of mental karma give rise to non-informative (avijñapti) matter, there are two interpretations within the commentary.
However, the *Yaoji* states:
"There is an interpretation; the Tripiṭaka Master explained it as follows:"
The fifty-three passages speak exclusively of the *manas-karman* (mental action) in terms of its active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
Based on this, it follows that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is established in reliance upon seeds (*bīja*).
Now, I shall investigate the intention of the Tripiṭaka masters.
Because the body and speech manifest [the intention] to others,
they are called manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*).
The seeds of volition (*cetanā*) do not manifest.
Therefore, it is called non-informative (avijñapti).
Mental action (manas-karman) is manifest only to itself;
thus, it can be said to be informative (vijñapti).
Because the seed does not manifest itself, it is also called "unmanifest" (avijñapti).
As stated in the *Fayuan*: "The second [type] says..."
One opinion holds that it gives rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*); another holds that it does not.
The latter explanation is considered correct.
The intention of the Tripiṭaka master lies in the former interpretation; this [latter] explanation is incorrect.
The *Fayuan* states that both interpretations may be used as one sees fit, yet it does not reject the latter explanation, taking its meaning to be definitive.
Now, according to my understanding, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) must necessarily arise;
since the Bodhisattva precepts fully restrain the three types of action (*trikarma*),
they are superior to those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) for as long as the future endures.
Why does one not produce the distinguished non-informative [action]?
The former two explanations are based on the neutral state;
they do not refer to the restraint (*saṃvara*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
Furthermore, that which gives rise to the essence of restraint is not itself restraint;
rather, it is called "restraint" by way of its fruit.
Therefore, what contradiction is there in the absence of unmanifest action (*avijñapti*)?
Therefore, [the opponent] now takes it that non-manifestation (avijñapti) is not produced.
But this is not so. Since you have already accepted that it is not produced, why do you say that while it can give rise to the substance of restraint (saṃvara), it is not itself restraint?
If it is argued that while the restraints of body and speech can be established, the restraint of mind cannot,
this is said from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, in contrast to the lack of such mental restraint in the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha).
The ten wholesome precepts and so forth are also forms of restraint (*saṃvara*).
How can it be said that their essence is not restraint?
Since they are named after their fruit, they lack unmanifest action (*avijñapti*).
Therefore, it is untenable. *Yaoji wen*:
Upon what dharma are the non-informative [actions] (*avijñapti*) of the meditative and the path-based intentions established?
The explanation says: Informative [action] (*vijñapti*) depends on present volition (*cetanā*).
Because the non-informative (avijñapti) depends on seeds,
it possesses both types [of causes],
unlike the bodily and vocal non-informative of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and the Path (mārga).
Question: If that is so, since the seeds exist after emerging from meditative absorption, one should establish the existence of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Answer: This is not analogous.
Because this morality that follows the mind (cittānuparivartin-śīla) is subtle when one has emerged from meditative absorption,
it does not establish non-informative action (avijñapti).
Alternatively, within a single moment of manifest volition (vijñapti-cetanā), there may be both informative and non-informative action.
This does not contradict the principle. Now it is said:
both the meditative (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*) mental states are invariably associated with non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), and they definitely grasp the present.
One must not say they are "delusive," for the precepts of meditative concentration and the path are concomitant with the mind;
whereas seeds exist even when the mind is absent, and thus are not concomitant with the mind.
Regarding the phrase "however, based on the limits of the good and evil of one's intentions and vows," Ximing states:
"Although vows are manifold..."
However, within this context, volition (*cetanā*) is said to be aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).

Regarding the claim that this contradicts one's own teachings: according to the Mahāyāna doctrinal system, it is essential that seeds be produced through the perfuming of actualized mental states (*samudācāra*).
Because these newly perfumed seeds possess powerful efficacy and are certain to bring about their results, they are termed "increasing" (*puṣṭi*).
As for the objection that, "If you now claim that seeds are established without being produced by perfuming (*vāsanā*) and increase moment by moment,
does this not contradict the various teachings of the Mahāyāna?"—
this is unreasonable.
It is not the correct interpretation to claim that the substance of the seed increases moment by moment;
this provisional explanation has already been clarified above.
If the capacity of the precepts were such that they invariably produce their results solely through the increase of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*),
then once the precepts have been relinquished, they should no longer produce results,
because their capacity would have been abandoned.
If the functional capacity is not relinquished,
then even at the time of death and so forth, the restraint remains established and is not termed "abandonment of the precepts," because the functional capacity still exists.
Therefore, through the power of the aspiration made at the time of the initial motivation,
once the seeds have been perfumed by manifest volition and the ritual of confession (śuklavidhi) and so forth has been completed,
[the result arises] upon those seeds by virtue of the force of that aspiration.
The non-informative (avijñapti) capacity that prevents and wards off all evils increases twofold at each stage; by means of this,
it causes volition (cetanā) to possess the functional power to produce karmic results.
The efficacy [of the action] is determinate;
it is not the case that the non-informative (avijñapti) itself, as a mere designation, can produce a result.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
Provisional phenomena are like non-existence because they are not [ultimately] produced by causes and conditions.
If one has abandoned the precepts,
one remains in accordance with that state, and the power [of the precepts] withers and ceases.

Because the karmic path has not yet been completed;

Because the seeds are able to prevent [the arising of] similar manifest actions.

If, after emerging from meditative absorption,
one is unable to restrain evil,
for this reason one does not guard against the preceding [factors] nor follows [the subsequent ones].
If the Prātimokṣa does not prevent transgressions, it exists only in the present moment;
however, if one has attained the clear precepts, it protects the root, the preliminary, and the subsequent [actions] all together.
The Path and meditative concentration both obtain possession across the three periods of time.
If their unmanifest [form] is the same,
then regarding the Prātimokṣa, there is only simultaneous and subsequent possession, but no prior possession.
Because the nature of form is dull,
when one relinquishes the precepts,
the subsequent precepts fall away and there is no further attainment of them.
This refers to non-existent post-attainment [wisdom].
Nevertheless, it belongs to the person who practices.
For instance, consider the case of relinquishing the precepts.
Although there is no acquisition of an acquisition,
because it belongs to one's own continuum,
it is nevertheless able to bring about a ripening fruit at a later time.
If one follows the path, concentration, and specific precepts of a Mahāyāna teacher,

If one abandons them at that time...
There are previously perfumed seeds capable of summoning subsequent fruits;
these are not separately designated as "dharmas" that are acquired before or after.
If one speaks of "before" and "after" in reference to the meaning of seeds, [it is as follows].

there is no textual authority stating that bodily and vocal informative actions (vijñapti-karma) are established only as unwholesome matter (akuśala-rūpa).
Although they cannot speak and so forth,
because their movements and other actions enable others to understand them,
the tenfold classification of informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter is explained in detail as set forth in the treatise.
Regarding the fifth section on the gates of acquisition and relinquishment:
first, the acquisition is explained;
subsequently, the relinquishment is explained.
The "attainment of clarity" is divided into two parts:
first, informative [action], and second, non-informative [action].
Informative precepts are not received from another.

Because at the time of the third *karmavācanā*, one simultaneously acquires the non-informative (*avijñapti*) precept; thus, the non-informative is common to both.

The first type, the *vargacārin*, also sees the Buddha.

Answer: From a remote perspective, this is also received from another. Question: If one has already received the prātimokṣa from another...
After attaining the noble turning of the mind and undergoing transformation for a long period until the attainment of Buddhahood,
one finally relinquishes the original body and its precepts;
yet, how could these not have been received from another?
Furthermore, it is the same for those who have attained the precepts prior to the tenth bhūmi. Answer:
According to the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna, even before the thirty-three moments of mind, the prātimokṣa belonging to the Buddha’s body is still termed "not yet attained."
After the thirty-fourth moment of mind, all that preceded it is relinquished,
because one has attained the superior and abandoned the inferior.
Consequently, there arises a distinct and new unmanifest (avijñapti) prātimokṣa.

Regarding this, there are two interpretations in the Mahāyāna:

That is to say, there are three grades of uncontaminated seeds within the mind:
namely, they are attained at the initial stage of the path of seeing as the inferior grade,
and are attained during the path of cultivation as the middling grade.
At that time, the Buddha attained the superior grade;
having abandoned the former inferior grades, only the superior grade remained.
How could this superior grade have been received from another?
Second, there is simultaneous abandonment through transformation.
For example, upon entering the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), when one transforms a lower grade [of defilement], one attains a middle grade;
if one attains a superior grade, one transforms the middle to attain the superior.
How could this superior grade [of the Prātimokṣa] also be derived from another?
Therefore, both Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas do not derive it from another.
Furthermore, the Pratimokṣa is divided into two categories: those who have attained it and those who have not.
This refers to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna,
as fully analyzed in the relevant chapters. Among the twenty schools, the three schools—

therefore, the Vinaya states that one simply requests the precepts by addressing the Sangha community, without mentioning a preceptor.
For what reason do these three schools maintain such a view?
Because these three were formerly companions of non-Buddhists,
they came to dwell together with the Saṃgha when they saw there was no gain or support;
later, laypeople sought to distinguish them from the rest.
Thereafter, they all shaved their heads.
Furthermore, the king sought to select those who had not received the precepts and would not permit them to remain.
All these people claim, "I have received the precepts.
The assembly of monks collectively rebuked them, asking: "From whom did you receive them?"

whereupon the people immediately said,
"Your preceptor is not pure."
"How is it that one obtains the precepts?"—

however, the other seventeen schools all reject it.
It must be pure and clearly abandoned within [the mind].
However, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "Committing a grave offense results in the loss of the precepts."
Nirvāṇa and others said:
"If one says that the precepts are lost, you do not understand my meaning;
if one says that the precepts are not lost, you likewise do not understand my meaning."
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is that there are two interpretations.
First, one who commits a grave offense does not lose their precepts.
As stated in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* and other texts: "If that is so, why does the Vinaya say it is like cutting off a person's head or shattering a stone? Answer:

This is because, according to the interpretation based on the *Yogācārabhūmi*, one loses the bodhisattva precepts only when there is an offense committed with an intense degree of mental affliction (*paryavasthāna*).
The middle and lower grades do not abandon [the practice].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* previously cited the superior grade,
while the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra* cites the middle and lower grades.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"My disciples who say that one who commits a grave offense abandons the precepts do not understand my intention;
furthermore, my disciples who say that one who commits a grave offense does not lose the precepts also do not understand my intention."
If you truly abandon your words, then you abandon your understanding of the Buddha’s intent;
if you truly do not abandon your words, then you do not abandon your understanding of the Buddha’s intent.
Since you have stated that you do not understand my meaning in either case, [you are at fault].

Therefore, it is known that the statement regarding "abandonment" refers to the superior grade of mind, while the statement regarding "non-abandonment" refers to infractions of the inferior and middling grades.
Thus, those who speak categorically of abandonment or non-abandonment do not understand the Buddha’s intent. The second interpretation states:
One who commits a grave offense abandons the precepts. Why is this?
The *Yogācārabhūmi* simply states:

Since the Bodhisattva precepts are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior, and do not mention separate liberation (prātimokṣa), it is known that [the Bodhisattva] relinquishes the precepts. Why, then,
does the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* state that one does not relinquish the precepts?
Speaking in terms of the provisional manifestation of transformation,
if one says that [the precept] has been violated,
then there would be no planting of the causes for cultivating goodness.
Because they do not show respect toward the monastic community, it is said that they do not commit an offense;
this is because the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks in terms of the provisional manifestations of transformation.
To say that they abandon [the teaching] without understanding my intent is incorrect.
Regarding the statement that "in terms of ultimate reality, one neither abandons nor resolves," the first master raises an objection:
"If this is so, why does the Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra state:
'If there are those who have committed a grave offense'?"
One who still remains within the monastery is called a "thief-dweller. Furthermore,
if such a person accepts even a single fruit as an offering from another,
they will certainly fall into hell.
Mañjuśrī asked, "How can one be born without fault?
The Buddha then spoke a mantra for him.
For one who recites this mantra, the precepts are restored to purity.
If they were abandoned entirely, how could one speak of their restoration to purity?
Thus, we know that there are degrees of lightness and gravity regarding the commission of grave offenses.
It cannot be definitively judged that all [precepts] are either to be relinquished or not relinquished.
Therefore, the Sūtra on the Precepts says:
"As it was before, so it is after."
One should thoroughly examine all the scriptural passages cited above; as for the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*),
if it is the antidote to what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) according to the Hīnayāna, [it is so].
Only in the six stages of the form realm;
for one who proceeds by way of sequential attainment,
it is only the initial preparatory stage.
If one is a transcender (atikrāntaka),
they enter both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation within the six stages, attaining the untainted (anāsrava) state.
Although these pertain to all nine stages,
the untainted discipline (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) and the discipline of restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) are not established in the formless realms (*ārūpya*),
because they are separated by a different realm (*dhātu*).
It is not established because there is no desire to be guarded against.
If, within the Mahāyāna, the untainted path of vision (darśana-mārga) were to enter the five stages of the form realm (rūpa-dhātu), [it would be as follows].
The Mahāyāna path of seeing relies upon the fourth dhyāna;
the same applies to the Pratyekabuddhas.
The non-informative matter (avijñapti) associated with these also follows accordingly as appropriate.
If it is the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) or the path of abandonment (prahāṇamārga) that is untainted (anāsrava),
it extends through the formless realm and the three lower stages.
Although there is the untainted in the stage of non-perception (asaṃjñī-bhūmi), it is not a path of abandonment.
If it is argued that untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas also prevent the sevenfold misconduct, we reply:

The treatise does not negate it as non-existent, but merely states that it is "not form. How is it "not form"?
This is explained in the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) of the eighteenth [chapter] on *nirvāṇa*.
One who contemplates the precepts says:

The thirty-sixth treatise on disputes states: "That which is called unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) is not a cause distinct from matter (*rūpa*).
It does not produce a result that is a distinct matter.

Regarding the statement "not having a cause different from form":
it does not mean that the primary elements (mahābhūtas) act as a direct cause by producing [form];
rather, it means they do not function as a cause for a result that is a distinct form.
It is not that the great elements (mahābhūta) are accepted as the cause of the result;
therefore, one should know that there is no actual "making," but that it is established solely based on volition (cetanā).
One should examine that passage.

2. This meditative absorption is not distinct from its basis; this is the objection regarding the identity of essence and function.

Because it is admitted that [the self] is subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), just like matter (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*citta*). This [argument] contradicts the formal inference (*prayoga*) of the non-Buddhist schools;

The statement contains two meanings;
therefore, the Master of the Treatise adopts the former meaning, while the opponent adopts the latter.
Furthermore, regarding the formal argument (pramāṇa) concerning the contradiction with the specific characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-viśeṣa-virodha*), it is stated as follows:
The dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are definitely substantially existent,
because they are detailed within the inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Just as with form, mind, and so forth,
it is stated directly that they definitely possess a real substance,

Therefore, it is not included within the category of "discrepancy regarding the distinction of the expression.

Since the formal argument (*prayoga*) was established by combining both [the reason and the example] as the cause (*hetu*), if an opponent were to say: "Matter, mind, and so forth possess real entities and functions distinct [from one another]," [the response follows].

The ten factors of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) depend upon the aggregate of morality (śīlaskandha) up to the aggregate of knowledge and vision (jñānadarśanaskandha). Among these,
the untrained right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of morality.
Right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*).
Right view, right intention, and right effort constitute the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).
These two are explained both in terms of their intrinsic nature and their attendants.
Right liberation is the aggregate of liberation.
Right knowledge is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, the treatises state that a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) possesses seven jewels; does he then possess the bodies of others or non-sentient things?
Ximing says: "If the Sarvāstivāda school admits this, it contradicts its own tenets.

Regarding how the Mahāyāna’s provisional attainment can be established in one case and not established in another, this is analogous to what has already been refuted.
