what fault is there in its application to both sentient and insentient beings, as well as to self and others?
This is because the sūtras contain statements regarding its "attainment."

If that were not the case, it would be no different from others and one could not avoid this difficulty. Question: If that is so, then the "accomplishment" (*pariniṣpatti*) of the distinct wheels may be explained as being due to the transformation of one's own consciousness;
but upon what basis is the "accomplishment" of other sentient beings and so forth provisionally established?
The answer is: We also allow that the *upādāya-rūpa* (supporting matter) of others undergoes transformation for the sake of enjoyment; therefore, it is also the object of one's own consciousness.
Furthermore, because it is produced by karma, it is provisionally established based on that karma, which is likewise not contradictory.
As for the statement that what has not yet been attained or what has already been lost should never arise again: [this refers to the specific conditions for its manifestation].
It is not yet obtained and can be known;
it is a dharma already lost.
Regarding future dharmas that ought to arise, they do not arise due to the deficiency of conditions.
It is also called "already lost," because this concentration will not arise,
as it has attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Just as dharmas already abandoned through the transformation of realms (*dhātu*) or stages (*bhūmi*) are termed "already lost," they are likewise permitted to arise.
This [dharma] has no prior acquisition (*prāpti*).
Now, regarding this class [of dharmas], since there is no prior acquisition, they should never arise.
As for the statement that "if it were to depend on other causes for its acquisition, then [the prior acquisition] would be useless," [it is as follows].
The mind that understands depends on four conditions;
material form depends on two conditions and is sufficient for the arising of dharmas.
Why then is there such prolixity in the arising [of consciousness]?
Therefore, it would follow that [the cause] is useless;
this refutation is not so,
for it is possible for a phenomenon to arise without being predominant.
However, the *Ryōjitsu-shū* (Essential Compendium) states:
"Is it not the case that the four causes and the five [factors] such as arising are easy to understand?

This should be verified by consulting the full text cited in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, where it is annotated in detail. Furthermore, regarding those who possess wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [states]: [the text continues].
In this regard, there is a general objection:
although there is no subsequent acquisition (*prāpti*) for that which has already been abandoned in the past, there is the simultaneous acquisition (*sahaprāpti*) of dharmas.
Regarding the future, there is both the loss of what has already been attained and the non-attainment of what has not yet arisen; furthermore, there is simultaneous attainment,
which makes it difficult for [the dharma] to arise, yet it can still be attained.
However, according to the original intent,
the difficulty lies only in the fact that the previously acquired [attainments] would not be lost and would manifest immediately;
thus, the phenomena of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) should manifest all at once.
As it says below: "If [the effect] were to depend on other causes, it would be useless;
if [the cause] has already ceased or if the conditions for the future world are lacking, [the effect] will not arise."
Although there is simultaneous acquisition, others maintain that it is useless because it cannot produce [the result];
thus, it would merely be a restatement of what is already established. As for those who claim that the present acquisition is not lost:
Although there are these two explanations,
according to the *Abhidharmakośa*,
who says that this acquisition (*prāpti*) acts as a cause for the arising of phenomena?
In the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*,
there is only the "non-disappearance" (*avipraṇāśa*) which serves as the cause for production;
therefore, that treatise states:
Because it is accepted that "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is the cause for not losing dharmas already obtained; thus,
according to two explanations in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
the correct position is likewise that it serves solely as the cause for non-loss.
[The opponent] argues: "Therefore, [the object] would be useless for both [the subject and the object] regarding the dharma.
Second, it is said that what is transformed by consciousness is not separate from sentient beings.
Thus, even insentient phenomena do not exist apart from sentient beings;
there is no such thing as a phenomenon that exists independently of sentient beings. This was stated first regarding the existence of attainment (*prāpti*).
Thereafter, there is nothing to be attained.

Question: Since it has been stated that non-existence is itself the absence of essence, what further phenomenon is designated by the name "detachment"? Answer: That very non-existence is conventionally designated as "detachment."
The absence of a substantial entity is called "separation from sentient beings.
To speak of the absence of intrinsic nature does not mean it is called "separation" simply because it is not established as a transformation of consciousness;
this explains the three kinds of establishment.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of phenomena:
first, those with substantial existence;
second, those without substantial existence. However, the establishment of accomplishment applies only to existent phenomena and not to non-existent ones.
Because there are no phenomena, no essence, and nothing that can be established, among existent phenomena there are further two kinds:
first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Furthermore, within the conditioned, there are again two kinds.
First, transformation of one's own consciousness;
second, transformation of another's consciousness. Within the transformation of one's own consciousness, there are further two kinds: first, seeds.
Second is actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).
Because seeds are hidden and difficult to perceive,
they are divided into these two categories.
First is the accomplishment of the seed;
second is the accomplishment of mastery.
Their manifestation is evident and easily understood.
Therefore, they are combined into one and termed "the accomplishment of active manifestation. Furthermore, within the seeds, there are three types:
first, the wholesome.
Two are unwholesome;
three are indeterminate. Among the wholesome, there are two:
first, the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Second, there are those with outflows (*sāsrava*). Within the wholesome states with outflows, there are again two kinds:
first, those consisting of preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Second is that acquired through birth.
The aforementioned untainted wholesome states and those resulting from application are both termed "mastery" (*vaśitā*),
because one who accomplishes these will necessarily attain mastery over birth and death.

Furthermore, because that which is produced through effort must necessarily involve the application of exertion before it can arise, it encompasses both the innate (*sahaja*) and the acquired (*prāyogika*).
Other meanings should be understood accordingly.
As for the wholesome obtained by birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*), it is acquired immediately upon birth.
Arising through habitual persistence,
those seeds that lack superior functional capacity are merely termed "attained at birth" (upapatti-pratilambhika).
Furthermore, unwholesome dharmas are likewise merely termed "accomplishment as seeds" (bīja-samanvāgama).
Because these dharmas cause one to sink into birth and death,
they lack the superior capacity for the factors conducive to liberation; thus,
although the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* speaks of the afflictions arising in Bodhisattvas of the ten stages...
The untainted [state] that arises in those who surpass the followers of the two vehicles is due to the bodhisattva’s untainted compassion and wisdom;
it is not something their own afflictions are capable of producing.
Therefore, it is not called "accomplishment through mastery. Within indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*), there are further two types:
first, obscured (*nivṛta*);
second, unobscured (*anivṛta*).
That which is obscured is explained in the same manner as the afflictions.
Furthermore, the unobscured-neutral is of four kinds;
the first is maturation (*vipāka*).
Second, the deportment;
third, the craftsmanship;
fourth, the transformation.
The ripening (vipāka) neutral [mind] consists solely of the possession of seeds;
the deportment (airyāpathika) and the skillful (śailpasthānika) each possess both types,
such as the gait of an elephant or the gallop of a deer.
The cultivation of fields, weaving,
and so forth are called the accomplishment of seeds;
it is like the gait of an elephant king.
The gait of the king of geese,
the carving of patterns, the inlaying of paintings, and so forth,
are called the accomplishment of mastery.
Because it must arise through deliberate effort rather than spontaneously,
transformational neutral [states] are established solely by sovereign power,
as they necessarily arise from functional exertion.
Furthermore, because one who has accomplished this attains mastery,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If it is wholesome [dharmas] produced through preparatory application (*prayoga*)."
And that portion of indeterminate seeds which is predominant is called "spontaneously accomplished" (*īśvarasamṛddha*).
The Abhidharma also says:
The wholesome dharmas of application refer to all mundane and supramundane functional capacities,
as well as a portion of the indeterminate.

This refers to the minds of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and transformation (*nairmāṇika*), and so forth; therefore, it was stated above that the transformation of one's own consciousness also extends to insentient things.
Some say this is because [the Buddha] creates the seven precious jewels.
If it is the transformation of another's consciousness, it should be understood according to the second case.
The transformation of the sense faculties and objects of others is discussed in two ways within the treatise;
this is explained in the seventh fascicle in the section analyzing the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It is also admitted that [the wheel-turning king] takes as an object the seeds transformed by others;
furthermore, it is said that a wheel-turning king accomplishes the seven jewels,
yet although these are transformed by others, they cannot be said to be "accomplished" [by him].
From the transformation of the staff perceived by one's own consciousness, it may also be metaphorically described as the accomplishment of three kinds. However, Ximing states:
according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
First, the nature of the differentiation of the continuum as comprised by the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
second, the nature of the differentiation of the continuum as arising through mastery;
and third, the nature of the differentiation of the continuum as arising through its own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Distinct from yoga,
the seeds are established as one,
while the manifest are divided into two.
The wholesome states resulting from application and so forth are termed "arising through mastery," not "arising through application."
It is merely that names arise from their own characteristics. Now, another interpretation states that this is the same as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
It says: "The two types of arising—sovereign arising and continuous arising—are distinguished by their specific natures."
When the seeds of wholesome dharmas such as preparatory application possess superior capacity and,
having given rise to actual manifestations, attain mastery, this is called "arising through mastery.
If both [the seed and the manifestation] manifest simultaneously, it is called "arising through self-characteristic."
Arising as actual manifestation is termed "arising of specific characteristics.
Regarding the establishment of unconditioned phenomena as "accomplishment," it is as explained in the original commentary.
Furthermore, the *Zhujie* (Explanatory Commentary) states:
According to the second [treatise],
there are two kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
First, based on the transformation of consciousness;
second, based on the establishment of suchness.
Can both be established? Yes, they can.
There are also three [points] where it is not so.
Answer: Since "acquisition" (prāpti) is established as a designation, both types coexist;
furthermore, there are distinctions such as seeds, mastery, and so forth.
Furthermore, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) is established based on the transformation of consciousness;
each is established upon its respective seed of vision (*darśana-bīja*),
because the seed serves as the cause that gives rise to the characteristics of the unconditioned phenomenon.
Alternatively, based on what is directly perceived, when the mind arises, it transforms that appearance;
thus, there are three distinctions.
When a wholesome mind of skillful means transforms [the object] and perfumes it to form a seed, this is called "accomplishment through mastery" (*vaśitā-nirvṛtti*).
The manifestation of mental transformations that are currently active constitutes manifest accomplishment (*sammukhībhūta-siddhi*).
All other mental transformations consist of the accomplishment of seeds (*bīja-siddhi*) and are not termed "mastery" (*vaśitā*).
If one establishes the proof based on suchness,
then "seed" refers to mastery (*vaśitā*),
while "manifest realization" refers to actual activity (*samudācāra*).
If it is subsequently obtained as an object,
it is explained in the same manner as that which is transformed by consciousness based on its prior support.
However, although non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not realized through wisdom, [it is nonetheless attained].
If one temporarily suppresses the afflictions and attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),

it is explained in the same manner as subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). If, however, there is no suppression of the afflictions and [the cessation] is manifested merely through the absence of conditions, [it is not so].
It is said that one attains those [attainments] based on the meaning of the non-arising seed;
the seeds of mastery and so forth should be understood according to their respective natures.
Furthermore, this is explained within the context of the basis for attainment.
The large and small [versions] differ,
as described in the original commentary (*shu*).
However, it is stated that the two belong to the "basis" (*āśraya*).

This refers to the eighth consciousness, such as dharmas that have attained ultimate non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the non-arising of erroneous principles within the Buddha-body, and so forth. Question: Since it is said that erroneous principles ultimately do not arise, [how can they be said to exist?]

It should be called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Why is it called "non-deliberative"? Answer: If something is permanently non-arising due to abandonment by means of wisdom, that is called "cessation through deliberation."
The false principles within the Buddha’s body are not eliminated through wisdom;
rather, because ignorance and the like have been severed,
those false principles do not arise.
Just as when entering the path of seeing,

the bodies of those in the Northern Continent and so forth do not attain non-analytical cessation; furthermore, it is explained that although these [defilements] never arise again in actual manifestation, they are nonetheless abandoned.
The seeds still remain and are likewise comprised within the obstructions;
it is only when the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) arises that the seeds are finally extinguished.
One immediately attains cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This attainment belongs to the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
If this were so, the mirror-like wisdom should be capable of abandoning defilements.
According to the true meaning, when the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) arises, it is not the support for those [afflictions],
as all contaminated (*sāsrava*) states have been abandoned; they are not severed through deliberate mental application (*manasikāra*).
It is not termed "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), nor can it be said to be abandoned by the wisdom of observation,
because it is not immediate [to that wisdom].
Because it is named "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue).
If one were still severing defilements,
one should be called "Equal Enlightenment" (Dengjue), just as [the stage immediately preceding it] is called "Uninterrupted" (Wujian).
Since it is not thus, when the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) arises, those [other cognitions] are spontaneously extinguished, attaining non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha);
this attainment belongs to the mirror-like wisdom.
However, the commentary states that it belongs to the eighth consciousness;
this is based on its dominant faculty (*adhipati-rāja*),
which is explained in terms of both cause and fruit.
If it pertains to the fruit of Buddhahood, it relies upon the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
This explanation was recorded as a direct transcription from what [the Master] heard personally.
Furthermore, it distinguishes between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna regarding their respective domains.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of attainment (*prāpti*): first,
the attainment of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and second, the attainment of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
If conditioned phenomena are attained,
they necessarily belong to that which is attained;
if that which is attained consists of the three natures.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) are also of three natures (*trisvabhāva*);
they belong to the three realms (*tridhātu*), the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), and consist of matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).

Furthermore, they are classified according to their respective realm and stage as appropriate. As for the acquisition of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): [it is of the same nature as that which is acquired].
There are three types of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as determined in the original commentary; however, they encompass both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
If attained through the six paths of practice, they are exclusively tainted.
The attainment of the path of seeing is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*);
that of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertains to both. This is because it is accepted that even on the path of cultivation, there is the abandonment of tainted states.
The path of no-more-learning is untainted;
the abandonment of the delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception occurs solely through the untainted path,
because one attains the fruit by relinquishing the stage of the candidate.
Upon abandoning the previous outflows, one gives rise to the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) thus acquired is invariably outflow-free.
However, the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is comprised solely within the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) that is maturation (*vipāka*).
[The opponent] considers both "arising" and "non-arising" to be substantial dharmas.
If the acquisition of arising belongs to the practitioner,
it is because it possesses substantiality.
According to what is appropriate,
one attains that which is to be attained and the path by which it is attained;
now, this non-analytical cessation does not arise due to the absence of conditions.
Since dharmas are not produced,
they cannot be attributed to that which is unproduced;
for they are not sentient beings.
It belongs solely to the nikāyasabhāga that serves as its basis.
As for non-acquisition (aprāpti),
it is established as belonging exclusively to the nikāyasabhāga that serves as its basis.
Concentration is exclusively of the nature of maturation and neutral;
however, if one has attained the dharma of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), it may still be regenerated.
Just as one who has fallen away from a fruit,
if they attain non-analytical cessation,
it will never arise again.
Because the conditions are lacking; if one follows the Mahāyāna,
the acquisition (*prāpti*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is likewise, like the Sarvāstivāda, strictly bound to that which is acquired.
The various natures, realms, and stages;
whether form or mind;
and the seeds and active manifestations of both outflowing and non-outflowing phenomena.
According to what is appropriate,
all [designations] are assigned to those respective phenomena based on what has been attained,
because they are conventionally established upon these various phenomena.
If it is the acquisition of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), it belongs to the same category as that [cessation] and is included within the path capable of attaining it;
however, it is exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
Because it is not admitted that the six modes of practice constitute the path of abandonment;
rather, it is only by relying on the Noble Path that the seeds are permanently destroyed and analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained.
Furthermore, the six paths of cultivation rely solely on the *anāgamya* stage and not on the fundamental stages;
they suppress the afflictions but do not eradicate them.
Because the seeds remain,
one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Furthermore, regarding the timing of the arising of the path that attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
there is a difference between the Great and the Small [vehicles].
As in the Sarvāstivāda school,
the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) serves as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
although it severs the afflictions, it coexists with the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those delusions.
As long as the "rope" of acquisition has not been severed, it is not yet called the attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

When the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises, it serves as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) precisely for the purpose of severing the rope of acquisition; although at that time one has not yet taken analytical cessation, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as an object of cognition or realization.
Based on this liberation, the acquisition (prāpti) of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is established.
Since the acquisition arises in anticipation to acquire that analytical cessation,
the acquisition of analytical cessation belongs to the path that is capable of acquiring it.
Because the knowledge of the patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti-jñāna) takes only the truth of suffering as its object and does not yet take cessation as its object—
since this analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is the truth of cessation—
the realization of this unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomenon is exclusively through the knowledge of inferior cessation.
Although the lower wisdom has been extinguished,
and the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the patience regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has also ceased,
one has not yet produced the possession (*prāpti*) that attains that unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
At the moment the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) arises, one attains the abandonment of those afflictions deluded regarding cessation;
it is only when the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is first attained that the "attainment of attainment" (*prāpti-prāpti*) arises,
because the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realizes it again immediately.

The rest should be understood accordingly. According to the Mahāyāna school, within the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the attainment through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-prāpti*) has not yet been established;
although one is correctly severing the afflictions and realizing what was previously unattained.
The seeds of the afflictions are fundamentally severed;
it is only upon the path of liberation that the "acquisition of acquisition" (prāpti-prāpti) arises.
It is based on this that the "acquisition of analytical cessation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-prāpti) is conventionally established.
Therefore, it is said below:
"Because the mental orientations regarding the period for severing delusions and realizing cessation differ;
or, based on the immediate [attainment], 'acquisition' (prāpti) is also provisionally established."
This is because it is realized through cessation.
Below, this is discussed in terms of the aspirational mind (*cittāśaya*), whereas here it is based on actual attainment (*prāpti*).
However, according to the Mahāyāna school, there are four truths, beginning with suffering (*duḥkha*).
Regarding the Four Truths, there are both phenomena and principle; in reality, there are three.
Although in truth there are not many, they are spoken of as four because they are established based on their designations.

The initial "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) constitutes the distinct realization of both the facts and the principles of the truth of suffering; however,
the reality realized therein is no different from that of the other four truths.
Why not simply designate this as the realization of the truth of cessation?
It is because, regarding the truth of cessation, one has not yet realized it through both its objective fact (*vastu*) and its underlying principle (*yukti*);
rather, it is the liberation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-vimukti*) that realizes the non-arising of those two obstacles, which constitutes liberation.
It is not that one only realizes the truth at this stage;
subsequent moments of mind should be understood accordingly.
Thus far, the characteristics of the seeing [of objects] have been explained in four distinct ways according to the meaning of the semblance path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
According to the reality of true insight, the four truths are realized simultaneously without sequence;
conversely, those who do not achieve this realization through such provisional designations are categorized,
within the defiled phenomena, into six pairs.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*,
even if the functional capacity is suppressed, it is still termed "non-arising," because the substance of the seed remains present.
This is also termed "accomplishment. It consists of:
first, the distinction between what is cultivated through seeing and what is cultivated through meditation; second, the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.
Third, the pair of manifest activity and seeds;
fourth, the pair of the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness;
fifth, the pair of afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions.
Regarding the six types of seeds and habitual tendencies,
first, as for those countered by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation:
these are the two obstacles consisting of all the conceptualizations of the three realms that exist on the paths of seeing of the three vehicles.
According to what is appropriate:
whether as seeds or as manifest, they are termed "non-accomplished.
Regarding the abandonment through cultivation within the three realms, they are termed "accomplished" or "non-accomplished" according to what is appropriate.
For the two vehicles, the designation "unaccomplished" applies to the afflictions of the path of cultivation that were previously suppressed during the path of seeing; conversely,
those not yet suppressed and thus not severed are designated as "accomplished."
Because it is not an antidote,
and because it does not obstruct vision; the same should be understood for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane:
the mundane path merely suppresses the greed, hatred, delusion, and pride that arise from the distinct heads of innate confusion regarding phenomena, preventing them from manifesting.
This is termed "non-attainment.
That which is deluded regarding principle and that which is subtle are not what is subdued;
this is termed "attainment."
The supramundane is as previously described.
Regarding the correspondence between active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds:
all active manifestations that have not yet arisen are termed "unestablished."
If it arises, it is termed "accomplished.
Regarding the seeds of the two obstacles: if they have not yet been impaired or suppressed, they are termed "established";
if they have already been severed, they are termed "unestablished."
If one is at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the substance [of the seeds] exists while their manifestation is established;
or, in cases where there is suppression, because the functioning of the suppressed seeds is impaired, they are also said to be unestablished.
If one is among the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), the seeds of the knowable (*jñeya*) are established.
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s attainment or non-attainment according to circumstances: as for the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, take for instance the afflictive hindrances;
for those in the stage of the Path of Seeing who follow the Two Vehicles, the delusions associated with the six [consciousnesses] that are conceptually discriminated are not attained.
The innate [afflictions] belong to both [categories].
The seventh is called "established.
Even if one gives rise to the fruit, one does not abandon the seven afflictions.
Within the path of cultivation, among the eighty-one categories [of afflictions], each may be either accomplished or not accomplished according to its respective condition.
If the seventh category of affliction is accomplished,
then only upon the abandonment of all eighty-one is it termed "not accomplished."
The abandonment of the first eighty [defilements] is still termed "accomplished" (*siddha*) from the perspective of possessing the seeds; however,
if one speaks in terms of functional capacity, it is termed "accomplished" through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
The supramundane [path] would not be established.
If one analyzes according to the six consciousnesses of a bodhisattva, the path of seeing (darśanamārga) would not be established;
however, it is established by way of the innate (sahaja).

Because there is no transcending of the fruit, within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), the six consciousnesses, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and so forth are permanently suppressed across the four stages; this is termed "non-accomplishment" (asiddha).
Prior to this, it is termed "accomplishment" (siddha).
Speaking in terms of function:
if one considers the substance of the seeds as they exist within the "name" (nāman), it constitutes the seventh [consciousness], the view of self;
at the moment immediately preceding the diamond-like samādhi (vajropamasamādhi), it is said that [the seeds] are no longer established.
What has been explained previously is termed "accomplished.
This is based on the essence of the seeds and does not refer to their function.

If one were to speak in terms of function, there would be both accomplishment and non-accomplishment; this much shall suffice for now. As for the opposition between afflictions and the objects of knowledge:
Regarding the obstacles to the objects of knowledge:
for the two vehicles, they are said to be accomplished;
for Bodhisattvas, they are both accomplished and unaccomplished.
Because, although those of the two vehicles have severed the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
the seeds [of these obscurations] still exist even though their active manifestations do not arise;
whereas for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), both types of dualistic discrimination are [eliminated].
The seeds of the afflictive obstructions that arise simultaneously with the path of cultivation are not eliminated by the path of seeing;
they are said to be eliminated prior to the moment immediately preceding the vajra-like samādhi.
Because the seeds are not severed.
If they are subsumed under the cognitive hindrances (jñeyāvaraṇa),
it remains undecided whether both the seeds and their manifestations are established or not.
In the Vajra-anantara [stage], both the seeds and the manifest forms of the two obstacles are termed "non-existent. Regarding the seeds and their latencies (*vāsanā*):
for those of the Two Vehicles, the latencies of the two obstacles are both present, because they do not sever these latencies.
For a bodhisattva, the seeds of afflictions that are co-emergent are termed "perfected.
The habitual tendencies of the two obstacles and the seeds of the cognizable are termed "perfected yet unperfected."
Because the seeds and habitual tendencies of the two obstacles are abandoned to a certain extent within the ten stages (*bhūmi*),
they are both designated as "non-existent" at the stage of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is a brief explanation.
A detailed analysis would be tedious; therefore,
regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas,
we shall first distinguish the retribution-indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) according to the realms (*dhātu*).
In whichever place one is born, both the seeds and the manifest [dharmas] are accomplished;
in other places where one is not born, the seeds are accomplished but the manifest [dharmas] are not. There is no arising of maturation (vipāka) in a different realm.
Furthermore, if it were severed, it would be the indeterminate (avyākṛta) maturation of humans or devas.
It is only upon reaching the vajrānantarya-moment or the path of liberation that one is said to be "not yet accomplished";
in all other stages, one is said to be "accomplished. This is stated with reference to the attainment of Buddhahood.
If it concerns those of the two vehicles, there is no non-attainment in the state of nirvana without remainder;
if it concerns the bondage of conditions,
it applies according to what is appropriate for each case.
Because it is adamantine, uninterrupted, and exhausts all delusions, it is called "unaccomplished.
This refers to those in the three miserable realms, eunuchs, women, long-lived devas, the non-conceptualizing devas (*asaṃjñisattva*), and so forth.
Once one has entered the path of seeing (darśanamārga), they never again arise;
this is called "non-attainment" (asiddhi).
Prior to that, it is called "attainment" (siddhi).
The previous explanation was based on manifest activity and functional capacity. However,
if one discusses the actual substance of the seeds,
they do not exist as a substantial entity within the matured results (*vipāka*) of the three miserable realms, nor do they exist at the stage of entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
In women and others, the seeds and the substance are termed "perfected" (*niṣpanna*).

Their deportment (*airyāpathika*) and indeterminate minds (*avyākṛta-citta*) pertain to both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), being perfected according to whichever of the two realms they are born into.
Both their seeds and their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are termed "perfected."
For those born in the formless realm, the seeds are established but not manifest;
the fruit of Buddhahood is not established.
The binding by conditions applies accordingly.
If one were to generically give rise to deportment, or even if deportment were produced through others' reception or transformation, it could still be termed "accomplished.
However, it would not be accomplished as a causal bond; it would exist only as a conventional designation based on the mind.
There is no real capacity to produce [them].

Even if they were real, the manifestation of the eight types of deportment (*airyāpathika*) from the eighth stage upward would not be established, because they are always untainted wholesome states and not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). As for indeterminate craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), it exists only in the Desire Realm; both its seeds and its manifestations are designated as "established."
If one is born in the two higher realms,
the two types [of vocal intimation] are accomplished as manifest but not as acquired;
although they possess speech, it is based on the body that they speak skillfully.
The two vehicles both achieve it;
the Buddha achieves neither.
From the eighth stage upward, the seeds are achieved but the manifest [attainment] is not.
If categorized according to the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*),
they should be understood accordingly as being associated with the neutral state of fruition (*nirmāṇacitta*).
They are established in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The ground-dharma belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because it supports those seeds and their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) below;
it is designated as "perfected" or "unperfected" according to what is appropriate.
If one reaches the fruit of Buddhahood, the seeds will finally not be produced.
If judged according to the bonds of conditions,
those of the Two Vehicles who have attained no-more-learning are also said to have unproduced seeds.
The seeds of the eighth stage are accomplished.

Within the wholesome states that are with outflows (*sāsrava*), there is the differentiation of the factors of birth; within the wholesome states of skillful means (*upāya*), there is the differentiation of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding their spheres and stages,
whether they are manifest or seeds, and whether they are established or not,
all such matters should be considered accordingly.
Regarding untainted wholesome states:
among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those without the [Buddha-]nature do not achieve them,
while those with the nature-seed (*gotra*) do achieve them.
The noble ones of the three vehicles possess both the seeds and the manifest activity [of afflictions].
Those of the two vehicles, however, lack both the seeds and the manifest activity in the state of nirvana without remainder.
Because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of other persons are exhausted at the time of *nirvāṇa*.
Question: It was previously explained that there is a basis for acquisition (*prāpti*); on what does non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) depend?
Answer: It is not established that the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of conditioned phenomena occurs as a manifest state;

rather, it is established based on seeds (*bīja*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that non-accomplishment (*asamanvāgama*) is established in contrast to accomplishment (*samanvāgama*) with respect to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Manifest activity is established as not depending on seeds;
non-possession (*aprāpti*) is the opposite of that.
Why does it depend on seeds? Furthermore, [the text] explains its dependence on seeds.
If one were to overturn that [position] and claim that the manifest does not depend on seeds,
then it would follow that it is neither established nor dependent; for just as seeds establish their own establishment by depending on seeds, so too must the manifest.
If it is not established, upon what could it depend?
Since its essence is not established,
it is simply without essence.
Second, the explanation of non-possession (*aprāpti*) according to one's own view:
whether it be the state of mastery or the seeds themselves, their presence in a state of incapacity is termed "non-possession.
This is also established based upon the seeds.
If that is so, what is the difference between this and non-possession (*aprāpti*) in the present?
This [case] refers to incapacity,
while that refers to not yet having arisen.
Therefore, there is a distinction.

If one considers them according to their essence, non-possession (*aprāpti*) is said to be identical to both types of possession—discriminative (*pratisaṃkhyā*) and non-discriminative (*apratisaṃkhyā*).
Within the context of the lineage (*gotra*), just as there are two meanings for the non-possession of the noble nature (*āryatva*).
First, the non-attainment of contradiction,
which is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
based upon the seeds of the two obstructions.
Second, they are mutually concordant;
this is explained in terms of their functional capacity.
False views sever the roots of goodness.
Alternatively, as long as one has not yet entered into the state of vision, even if seeds exist,
they are also said to be unestablished because they have not yet begun to exercise their functional capacity.
It is provisionally established based on the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).
Its manifestation is not established independently, but is likewise established based on the seeds.
It is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
The unconditioned state of analytical cessation;
persons lacking the spiritual lineage;
and those who have not yet entered the path of seeing.
All are established based on the seeds of the two obstacles.
From the moment one enters the path of seeing onwards,
the two obstacles arise simultaneously according to what has not yet been abandoned.
The non-acquisition of analytical cessation is established because one has not acquired that analytical cessation which is realized [by the path];
the non-analytical non-acquisition is likewise established according to the circumstances.
It is established based on those various conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) in their seeds and manifestations,
because it brings those phenomena to completion;
it cannot be obtained through non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

Regarding the statement that "the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) is a nominal designation and not a substantial entity," this nature of an ordinary person is analyzed through three approaches.
First, the explanation of its name.
Second, the essential nature;
third, the distinctions.
Regarding the explanation of the names:
First they separate and later they reunite.
There are two types of difference:
first, that which is called "distinctness" is difference.
This means that while noble ones (ārya) are born only in the two destinies of humans and devas,
this [state] extends to all five destinies,
unlike the case of the noble ones.
This is categorized according to the differences in destinies (*gati*). It also encompasses the four modes of birth (*yoni*);
these four modes of birth are not the same.
Second, they differ in name because of their transformation;
for while this transformation leads to wrong views and the like,
all noble ones (ārya) equally possess right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
This is based on the differences in views.
This also includes distinctions regarding the objects apprehended and the manner in which those objects are apprehended.
"Arising" (jāti) refers to the process of origination and the categories of beings.
This refers to the arising of differences among destinies (*gati*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*).
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) means essential nature (*svabhāva*).
It is by virtue of this nature that destinies and views are differentiated.
The above explains the term "ordinary" (*pṛthagjana*).
Those belonging to the class of beings distinct from the Sages are called "ordinary beings.
The term "beings" (*janman*) is a general designation.
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) here refers to a distinction.
The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is called "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
This is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Furthermore, the forty-fifth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* largely agrees with this explanation.
Therefore, the Venerable Vasumitra stated:
"It causes sentient beings to give rise to views of a different category and afflictions of a different category."
Because one creates karma of a different category,
undergoes the fruit of a different category,
and is born into a different category of existence.
Regarding the term "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*): second, concerning the essential nature [of this state],
first the divergent views are presented,
followed by the Mahāyāna position.
Regarding the presentation of alternative views:
the Vātsīputrīya school asserts that its essential nature consists of the ten afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, [this entity] possesses a distinct substantial nature that is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta),
is bound to all three realms,
and is dissociated (viprayukta).
The Sautrāntikas do not establish it as having a separate substantial nature;

rather, they provisionally designate the term "nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*) with respect to the specific state of the continuum of one in whom the noble dharmas have not yet arisen.
Although the Mahāyāna is likewise included within the category of non-associated [factors],
it does not possess a distinct substantial nature apart from form and mind;
rather, it refers to the state prior to the permanent abandonment of the seeds of the two obstacles upon their severance.

The designation "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not established solely on the basis of the non-arising of all noble dharmas belonging to one's own vehicle due to an obstacle;
for those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*), there is no distinct obstacle [to such arising].
This is established solely in reference to the fact that the seeds of the afflictions of insight have not yet been severed;
it is because one has not attained the noble dharmas,
whether in terms of their function or their essence.
It is said that both fail to achieve [the goal]:
those with the spiritual lineage do not accomplish the functional utility,
while those without the spiritual lineage do not even achieve the essential nature.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 52) states:

"The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is defined as the mere state in which the seeds of what is to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms have not yet been permanently destroyed. This is a conventional designation established upon the seeds of both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
This treatise also states:
"In the state where the seeds to be abandoned through vision within the three realms have not yet been permanently destroyed,
the designation 'non-attainment' (aprāpti) is provisionally established as the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva)."
Nor does it say that each [obscuration] specifically obstructs the manifestation of its own noble lineage (*āryagotra*);
rather, it simply states that one has not yet accomplished the various noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
As for the distinctions, there are two types of distinctions regarding the five vehicles.
First, the distinctions are established;
subsequently, they are clarified through questions and answers.
For now, the Mahāyāna is definitively determined.

The nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) in the Mahāyāna is established based on the seeds of conceptual discrimination that have not yet been permanently severed, which depend upon both obstacles.
This is provided that the cognitive obstacle (jñeyāvaraṇa), being ultimately indestructible, is not a mental affliction (kleśa).
Based on these afflictions,
one portion is established as the fixed nature of śrāvakas,
and another portion is established as the fixed nature of pratyekabuddhas, both being the nature of ordinary beings.
Because one contemplates the truths and the twelve links of dependent origination,
and realizes them through the distinction between the two natures of dependence and reliance,
if both were not subject to cessation, [enlightenment would be impossible].
Based on this, the nature of ordinary beings of the Vehicle of No-Nature is established. Regarding those of indeterminate [lineage]:

if there are those who, possessing the requisite conditions for contemplating the truths and dependent origination, attain the supramundane, then based on all their conceptualized afflictions, the nature of ordinary beings of the two vehicles of indeterminate lineage is established.
If there are those who, by relying on the four truths and the six perfections, attain transcendence,
they are established as being of indeterminate śrāvaka or ordinary person (pṛthagjana) nature.
If there are those who, by relying on dependent origination and the six perfections, attain transcendence...
Based on this, one is established as having the indeterminate nature of a solitary realizer (pratyekabuddha) or an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).

If one possesses the nature of the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) categorized as inferior, middling, or superior, one is established as having the indeterminate nature of a śrāvaka, a solitary realizer, or an ordinary person. This is because the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* speaks of entering the Dharma through five types of spiritual lineages (gotra).
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that they are established as having the nature of not attaining parinirvāṇa, the nature of a śrāvaka, and so forth;
thus, these distinctions are established through mutual contrast. Based on this meaning, one should formulate a fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are those who possess only the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and do not possess the nature of an noble one (*āryatva*),
namely those of no spiritual lineage (*agotraka*).
There are also those who possess only the nature of an noble one and do not possess the nature of an ordinary person.
From the Mahāyāna path of seeing onwards,
there are those who have both attained the nature of an ārya and the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana);
this is based on the seeds [of the three vehicles] prior to the path of seeing.
There are untainted seeds that also constitute the nature of an ārya;
however, whether they have already arisen or have not yet arisen in the present, they are termed "not established.
This is not stated with reference to the seeds themselves.
Alternatively, the noble nature (*āryatva*) is established solely on the basis of that capacity to produce manifest activity,
because it is defined by its contrast with the opposite state;
otherwise, the mere seed would not constitute the attainment of the noble state.
If it were taught that they exist only in the present,
then when an noble one’s untainted [state] does not arise in the present,
that person would be neither an ordinary being nor a noble one.
If one follows this explanation,
those of the three vehicles with fixed natures prior to the path of seeing are also said to consist solely of the category of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Those of the two vehicles who have attained the state of an ārya, as well as those who have turned toward the Mahāyāna but have not yet entered the first bhūmi, are said to be both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and to possess the nature of an ārya.

Those of the two vehicles in the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* belong to the category of "neither. Regarding the analysis through question and answer: Question: What of those with the fixed nature of the Mahāyāna and those with the indeterminate nature who are capable of proceeding toward the Mahāyāna?
The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established based on the seeds of the two obstructions.

Regarding the question of whether those of fixed lineage among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are also included as bases for these two [obstructions], there are two interpretations.
One says that it is established based solely on the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because those [obstructions] are neither severed nor obstructed. Question: If they do not obstruct severance, then they cannot serve as a basis for establishment.

For a person of no lineage (*agotra*), since the two obstructions are neither severed nor obstructed, that vehicle should likewise not be established as a basis. Answer: Because the obstructions are extremely heavy. If that were so, then persons of fixed lineage in the two vehicles would be unable to proceed toward the Great Vehicle.
Is that cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) also called "extremely heavy"?
If it is called extremely heavy, it should likewise be established based on [the nature of] reliance;
if it is not called heavy, it is because it does not obstruct the fruit of its own vehicle.
The same applies to those without lineage (*agotra*).
Answer: Those with a fixed lineage (*niyata-gotra*) can attain the state of an *ārya*.
Although they possess knowledge, it is not termed "repetition" (*punarukta*).

Because those without lineage cannot attain the state of an ārya, the two obstacles are termed "heavy. Question: Afflictions (*kleśa*) can be severed, whereby one attains one's own vehicle; thus, afflictions are not termed "heavy.
However, the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are not to be severed, yet without them being attained, the Great [Vehicle] is not realized. Why then are they termed "heavy"?
The obscuration regarding the objects of knowledge is also called "heavy.

If the objects of knowledge do not obstruct [the path], then the two obscurations do not obstruct ordinary beings. Answer: That which possesses only the dharmas of an Arya is called "Arya-nature" (āryatva).
Those with fixed natures whose objects of knowledge are not obstructed are light;

because those without lineage will ultimately lack the noble dharmas, their two obstructions are called heavy. Question: If one considers all noble dharmas in relation to them, they are termed the "noble nature."
Because it does not obstruct, it is called "light.

Furthermore, all obstructing dharmas should also be called "ordinary beings" (pṛthagjana), and one should abandon them all upon attaining the nature of a noble one (ārya). Answer: Both types of knowledge are capable of realizing the principle.
The noble lineage (*āryagotra*) is simply the possession of the noble dharmas;
it is the determined nature of what is to be known, which is never subject to abandonment.
It does not obstruct the noble dharmas, nor is it the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
If one were to establish the attainment of the state of an Arya based on the claim that the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned,
it would contradict the various treatises which state that only the great [bodhisattvas] alone abandon the cognitive obstructions.
If they cannot abandon them, and yet you grant that the obstruction still persists, how could they possibly attain the nature of an Arya?
From this it is known that [the designation] is established based solely on one [factor]. For example,
when the cognitive obstacles (jñeyāvaraṇa) exist within the bodies of those of the two vehicles, they are not termed "obstacles."

Because that which does not obstruct its fruit is termed "unobscured" (*anivṛta*). If that were so, then the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) belonging to the lack of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) would also not obstruct it, and thus should not be termed "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*). Answer: Humans and devas are alike [in being] ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
It does not obstruct and it cannot defile.
One who stands in contrast to the noble ones is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Because they have not attained [the noble state], they are said to be defiled. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although it does not obstruct people, [it still defiles them].
It is called "defiled" because it arises through feeling;

it does not obstruct the limited [knowledge] of what is to be known, nor does it produce rebirth, and thus it is non-defiled. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that even those of fixed lineage among the two vehicles establish the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) based on the two obstacles.
Because there is no scriptural statement [to the contrary], and because it must necessarily prevent the attainment of the Great Vehicle;

just as the obstacle of lacking the spiritual lineage (agotra) necessarily prevents the attainment of the state of an Arya, for these two are established based on the two [types of obstacles]. If that is so, do the followers of the Two Vehicles eliminate this "nature of an ordinary being" (pṛthagjanatva), which is an object of knowledge? Answer: There are two interpretations.
One says: "It is also abandoned. If that were so, it would follow that the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) must also be abandoned. Answer: Granting this, there is no fault.
It is like the abandonment of the obstructive afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); yet this case is not the same.
The hindrances to meditative concentration are removed from their manifestation, but not from their seeds;
this is because it relies upon the seeds. Answer: Although it is established in reliance upon the seeds, it does not directly grasp the seeds themselves.
The designation "lineage" (gotra) is established based on seeds.
The statement that "the objects of knowledge are not severed" is spoken in reference to the substantial nature of the seeds;
the statement that "the lineage of ordinary beings is severed" is spoken in reference to its conventional functional capacity.
Since the provisional and the real are distinct, they do not contradict one another.

According to this interpretation, even those who have not yet attained certainty as śrāvakas are called "noble ones" (ārya), because they have abandoned the nature of an ordinary being (pṛthagjanatva) upon attaining the state of a noble one. One opinion holds that [the nature of an ordinary being] is not severed.
From the perspective of one's own vehicle, it is said that one attains the nature of an ārya.

However, as long as the objects of knowledge have not been abandoned, that lineage (gotra) still persists. If this were so, one would have to be called both an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and an ārya. What fault is there in admitting this? There is the fault of confusion. [The opponent asks: If the nature of an ārya were the very same as the nature of an ordinary person, then confusion would indeed occur.
If the two natures are distinct, how can there be no confusion? Although the two natures do not intermingle, ordinary beings and sages do.
Answer: From the perspective of their respective meanings, they are distinct;
thus, there is no fault.
Just as noble beings of the two vehicles who are of indeterminate nature are also called "distinct from the small" even before reaching the first bhūmi, the latter explanation is therefore correct.

Question: Why is it not established based on the innate obstacles (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*)? Answer: Because [the innate obstacles] are capable of completely obstructing the untainted (*anāsrava*) paths of both seeing and meditation.
Because it is established as being co-nascent with all obstacles and because it is not established based on [the presence of] the two types of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*),
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (56) states:
"It refers to the state in which all supramundane noble dharmas (*lokottara-āryadharma*) have not yet arisen."
The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established.

This treatise also states that the state in which the seeds to be abandoned by seeing have not yet been permanently destroyed is conventionally designated as "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*), and this is called the nature of an ordinary person. Question: Is the nature of an ordinary person established based on the seeds to be abandoned by seeing?
Is it not established based on the seeds to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) throughout the three realms? Answer: There are two interpretations.
One says that only the eighth [consciousness] in its active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) is taken.
It is established based on the seeds to be abandoned by insight within the same stage; it is not established based on all seeds of conceptual construction.
Otherwise, a single realm would become three realms.
They should be called "ordinary beings of the three realms.
If one takes the seeds of the manifest arising [of afflictions],
then having already attained the higher meditative absorptions, one gives rise to the afflictions of the higher stages.
They are also called "ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the three realms.
One interpretation states that this refers generally to the seeds to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms,
as the text contains no qualification to the contrary.
Since they are equally ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
there is no confusion; they do not share the same essential nature (*svabhāva*) as those belonging to different realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), or modes of birth (*yoni*).
The realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and births (*yoni*) and so forth manifest the distinctions between realms and destinies;
because these differ from those of the noble ones (*ārya*), they are not intermingled.
The previous explanation is correct.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56, states: "Because there are distinct natures (*gotra*) for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the three realms;
since nature belongs to birth, and birth is already differentiated by realm."
Therefore, birth is also distinct. Question: From the perspective of the noble ones looking toward ordinary beings, all untainted states constitute the nature of the noble ones;
from the perspective of ordinary beings looking toward the noble ones, [how is this so?]

Question: Are all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)? Answer: Contaminated phenomena arise even for noble ones (*ārya*). However, it is not the case that contaminants belong to ordinary beings.
By analogy, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena are entirely absent in ordinary beings.
Therefore, it is collectively termed the "noble nature" (*ārya-dhātu*). Second, distinguishing [this] from the Hīnayāna:
first, regarding the sixfold distinctions according to the Sarvāstivāda school. First, the distinction of basis (*āśraya*):
the Sarvāstivādins maintain that [the noble nature] depends solely upon the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

The Mahāyāna establishes [the abandonment] based on the seeds of the two obstacles; thus, the distinction between the provisional and the real can be understood. Third is the distinction regarding the stage of abandonment.
The Sarvāstivādins have three explanations.
The first states that it is abandoned at the stage of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).

One view holds that it is abandoned at the moment the arising-phase (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) of the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) occurs, because the afflictions are severed precisely at the time of its cessation.
Another view holds that it is abandoned by both [the arising and the cessation phases].
Just as the two paths of liberation immediately follow the abandonment of afflictions in cutting off delusions, so too,
according to the Mahāyāna masters, at the very moment the true vision arises, it is simultaneously ceasing.

The "path of seeing as conventional designation" (prajñapti-darśanamārga), which consists of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*), is metaphorically called "abandonment.

This means that they have not obtained anything at all, because it is not specified otherwise.

Since these are established based on the obstructions,
when one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), the two types of conceptual discrimination are severed; thus,

Because they exist substantially apart from consciousness, like [the marks of] form and so forth.

because the Mahāyāna masters do not admit that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) can sustain the body.
If it is granted that the body can serve as a support,
this refutes the Sautrāntika position that the category of consciousness is perfumed;

Treatise:
Regarding the threefold classification of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) according to their specific meanings—

just as the four right efforts are explained as four in terms of meaning while their essence is diligence (*vīrya*), and although there are three [aspects] such as life-force and so forth, they are one in essence when categorized by meaning— the opponent raises this objection:
Longevity and so forth are explained according to their meaning;
in essence, they are divided into three aggregates.
Right abandonment is categorized according to its significance.

Question: Why is the faculty of life (*jīvitendriya*) classified under three bases (*āyatana*), while the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are subsumed under a single base? Answer: Because the faculty of life is distinguished by its specific meaning and possesses a distinct preeminence, it is divided across three bases;
whereas the right efforts, being distinguished only by their general meaning and lacking a distinct preeminence, are gathered into a single base.
Furthermore, although it is not entirely similar, a partial analogy is employed.
The treatise states: "That which ceases is the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), not the *ālayavijñāna*.
An external objection is raised as follows:

As stated in the *Śūyao* (Essential Summary), the exposition on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is correct.
Within the various teachings of the Mahāyāna, there are six different [positions]: first, those that speak exclusively of the seeds of the eighth consciousness.
Thus, this treatise presents two general explanations.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
"The seeds of the eight faculties are established as being present and determinate."

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is included in the middle [category]; the three [faculties of pleasure, pain, and equanimity] are exclusively among the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*). The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (First Chapter) states:

"The life-faculty refers to the determinate duration of the abiding of the six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), which are the maturation (*vipāka*) projected by prior karma. The four [faculties of faith, vigor, mindfulness, and concentration] pertain to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter one, states:
"What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?

The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states:
"Homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) refers to the continuity of the aggregates throughout a single lifetime. This fifth [category] is explained according to its general characteristics.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 52, states:
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?

It is the measure of duration and the force of persistence belonging to the self-body produced in various locations; this is what is called "life. This is explained in terms of the six bases of maturation (*vipāka*).
The fifty-sixth [fascicle] states:

"The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is established as the state of certainty during the duration of the maturation (*vipāka*) projected by karma. This accords with the *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifest), as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*).
The determination of the eight faculties is as in the *Jiyao hui* (Essential Summary).
All other passages do not contradict the preceding three [points]. However, there is another interpretation in the *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifest) which states:
"Although the characteristics (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) are distinct, they are not separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

The objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of this consciousness is collectively termed "this consciousness. Furthermore, it is said that the mental faculty (manas-indriya) is able to sustain the five faculties;
when the sustainer and the sustained are explained separately, they are called the "six bases" (ṣad-āyatana).
There is no contradiction in this treatise’s combined explanation of the subject and object as being the seeds of this consciousness;

although there are various commentaries, the sub-commentary definitively concludes that only the seeds of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness are designated as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The interpretation that "it does not grasp the aspect" is correct.
As for the explanation regarding how this can be so when one has reached the formless realm (*ārūpya*), it is as follows:

Since material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are solely objects of aversion,

Because mental factors are universally capable of producing revulsion,

material phenomena, however, are solely objects of revulsion.
It is said that mental phenomena (citta-dharma) are called "formless" (arūpa).
These very mental phenomena are collectively capable of producing weariness [with cyclic existence].

Form-phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are solely objects of aversion;

This is stated in succession to further clarify and assist the understanding of the preceding text.

Disgusted with the mind, one enters the mindless.

That which is established separately as neither form nor mind is called "mindless.

There exists something distinct that is neither form nor mind, which is called "formless" (*ārūpya*).

Treatise:
At the stage of the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*), the perfuming of the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) establishes the seeds for a mind of revulsion.
Why, then, is the "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*) not established at this very stage?
It is only upon reaching the subsequent moment that it is designated as the "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*), for the preceding and succeeding moments are equal. Ximing states:
"The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha says only that it is established based on seeds."
This does not avoid the previous difficulty;
for it is now stated that the two meditative attainments are provisionally established based on their seeds.
Therefore, although they have achieved the seeds, because the conditions are not yet complete, [the attainment does not arise].
The two meditative attainments are not established independently; they are established only by waiting for the cessation of the mind,
just as when the seeds of the non-informative [matter] of restraint are first formed.

Because the conditions are not yet complete, the non-informative (avijñapti) is not established. Now, it is said that there is no difficulty even in the interpretation of the True Meaning (Paramārtha):
although there is no mind, there is the seed as a basis;
since at the initial moment there is the capacity to perfuse, it is not yet a state of no-mind, and thus it is called "based on seeds."
This is fundamentally for the purpose of generating aversion;
while the mind has not yet been established,

Treatise:

Because one seeks the fruit of non-conceptualization prior to the attainment of the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the seeds perfumed thereby bring about that maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna).
Regarding this, there are two interpretations in the original commentary.
One personally abandons the prior correct [view].
Although there is no actual ripening of the fruit of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*), as it is merely nominal and not truly productive of karmic result,
one nevertheless cultivates the meditative attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in order to seek that fruit.
If it were the case that the state of having a mind could produce that fruit of non-conception,
why would one need to cultivate a concentration without mind?
For it is by the seeds perfumed by the extremely subtle mind immediately preceding the concentration without mind that [the fruit] is produced.
Only when the mind is prevented from arising can it be called the "mindless concentration" (*acittaka-samādhi*).
This means that a provisional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*) is able to prevent the substantial mind.
When the fruit is subsequently attained, although that [provisional phenomenon] remains provisional, [it has fulfilled its function].
However, because of the power of the mind of revulsion,
although ideation and so forth do not arise, they are metaphorically described as being "experienced.
What contradiction is there in this principle?
If both [the seeds of the mind and the seeds of the formless attainments] were truly capable of producing [the resultant consciousness],
then it would be identical to the eighth [consciousness] and could not be called "mindless.
Furthermore, this treatise merely states that the seeds perfumed by causes invite that resultant maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Based on this, because coarse and mobile perceptions and so forth do not function, "non-perception" (asaṃjñika) is provisionally established;
it is not said that a seed is produced which brings about that non-perception.
Furthermore, this [state] is merely provisional.
How does the seed produce its result? Question: At the time of attaining the fruit, the subtle mental seeds have long since ceased;
there exists only a continuous stream of non-mental seeds, and not two kinds of seeds.
How can it be said that a mind with outflows (sāsrava) brings about a result with outflows? Answer:
Although there is no separate seed, the final moment of consciousness itself, together with its seeds, is cultivated simultaneously;
it possesses the power to bring about the collective maturation (vipāka) of those [results].
Because it is not yet matured, the fruit cannot arise;
later, when the matured fruit is about to manifest from the seed,
looking toward the time the fruit is obtained, it is said that there is a mind that experiences [the result].
Therefore, this does not contradict the statement in the *Ximing*:
"It should be understood that these seeds— whether minute (*sūkṣma*), very minute (*atisūkṣma*), or even more minute (*atisūkṣmataras*)— added during the stage of preparation (*prayoga*),
all induce a collective fruit consisting of a mental (*sacittaka*) maturation (*vipāka*)."
In the state of true non-consciousness (*acittaka*), the fundamental actual seeds (*mūla-bhūtāni bhūtāni bījāni*) project a distinct fruit that is itself non-conscious.
It is a settled principle that the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) obstructs the arising of the mind;

there is no need for further confusion. Although this is a divergent interpretation, it accords with the original explanation insofar as the capacity to project [the fruit] according to its timing does not exceed it.
However, there is yet another fault.
What is it? You yourself admit that those heavens are not produced fruits and lack a distinct substantial entity;
therefore, they should not be said to be actual seeds that produce [results].
If it is admitted that [the result] is actually produced,
why then do you further say that the power of concentration without mind obstructs the arising of the mind?
This principle is certain.
To labor in vain; the *Yaoji* states:
"Some say there are two interpretations, and that the latter contradicts [the *Śāstra*] 56. The *Benshu* itself judges that the latter explanation is not the correct one."
Why trouble to state it again? Nevertheless, it is said that the eighth consciousness as the collective retribution of those heavens,
as well as the mind acquired at birth and so forth,
must necessarily be induced by the seeds of the extremely subtle conscious mind.
If there were no present volition,
the seed could not independently take up its fruit; thus,
that which is metaphorically termed the "ripening" (vipāka) is a distinct retribution separate from the state of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
That is to say, the fruition is explained as occurring simultaneously according to its respective basis;

it is impossible to divide the seeds of the two states—possessing mind and lacking mind—and claim they produce two distinct fruits separately. Since the fruition occurs at one time, how could one state possess mind while the other lacks mind?
Furthermore, if they were to arise simultaneously, there would have to be no state of mindlessness, as [the seeds] would be acquired at the same time as the total maturation (vipāka).
Why then do you speak of "before and after"? If you say, "Who says there is before and after?", this contradicts the treatise which states that the mind and mental factors cease [simultaneously].
Since it has already been stated that the mind and mental factors cease,
it is clearly understood that their initial arising as active manifestations likewise cannot be spoken of.
In the *Abhidharmakośa*, fascicle 56, it states that "arising" refers to the volition (*cetanā*) capable of inducing the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
which is able to bring about its corresponding ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*);
this clarifies that they occur at one and the same time.
It is not the case that the general and specific fruits are separately distinguished; this [case] is likewise not so.
If one were to take the treatise literally, then present volition alone would be required, and it could not be extended to include seeds.
He [Vasubandhu] says that it is the volition capable of inducing the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)—
that is, the manifest volition— that induces it,
and he further does not mention seeds.
If it is said that seeds are understood through their meaning,
then by taking this meaning, one speaks of the "inducing of the aggregate retribution.
Based on this aggregate retribution, the six consciousnesses do not function, and thus "non-conception" is provisionally established.
Therefore, this treatise states:
"Thus, the seeds perfumed therein bring about that ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*);
based upon it, because coarse and mobile perceptions and so forth do not function, one conventionally designates it as 'non-conceptual' (*asaṃjñin*)."

The treatise states: "From before the attainment of the non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) until the point it draws forth its resultant maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna), it clarifies the basis;

Question: Regarding the establishment of the cessation of the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*), how many consciousnesses are established as ceasing? Answer: It is established by the cessation of one consciousness.
This is because the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body exist only in the first dhyāna;
in the fourth dhyāna, they are merely coarse and belong only to the sixth [mental] consciousness.
It is impossible for the three consciousnesses of the eye and so forth, which are the maturation (vipāka) of lower stages, to arise there.
Therefore, it is only the sixth [consciousness]. Question: On what stage does that resultant consciousness take as its object? Answer: It takes as its object the stage in which one is born.
This is because the craving that moistens rebirth must necessarily belong to the same stage as that which is being reborn.

It is not said that the moisture of craving for one stage causes birth in another stage. Question: Since the fruition of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya*) is established based on what is loathed, why are the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) established based on what is able to loathe? Answer: Because the fruition is that which is sought after.
Regarding that which is sought, the maturation (vipāka) is established;
likewise, the meditative absorption (samādhi) is also sought.
Thus, upon the basis of two absorptions, two further absorptions are established.
Therefore, there is no fault or difficulty.
